Forthwith means immediately — right now, without any pause, delay, or hesitation. When something must be done forthwith, it must be done straight away. There is no "I'll do it later," no asking for more time, and no acceptable reason to wait.
It's Not Just Any Word for "Immediately"

Here is where it gets interesting. Forthwith does not simply mean "quickly." It carries a formal, commanding, authoritative weight that ordinary words like "right away" or "at once" do not have.

Think of it this way: if your friend says "do it right away," it feels casual and friendly. But if a judge reads from a court order that something must be done forthwith, it feels serious, binding, and non-negotiable. The word itself signals: this is an official instruction, and delay will not be tolerated.

That combination — immediacy + formality + authority — is what makes forthwith unique.
Where You Will See or Hear It

Forthwith lives almost entirely in formal and official settings. You will typically encounter it in:

  • Court orders and legal documents — this is its most natural home
  • Official government notices and letters
  • Formal written instructions from someone in authority
  • Classic and older literature (19th-century writers like Charles Dickens used it freely)
  • Formal speeches where someone wants to sound commanding and serious

You will almost never hear it in everyday conversation. If someone said "eat your vegetables forthwith!" at the dinner table, it would sound theatrical and almost comical — because the word is simply too grand and official for casual settings. That reaction itself tells you a lot about what kind of word it is.

"The court ordered that the prisoner be released forthwith."
→ The court is demanding release right now. No unnecessary delays, no stalling. The order takes effect immediately.

"You are hereby instructed to vacate the premises forthwith."
→ Leave now. Not tomorrow, not after you've slowly packed everything. Leave with maximum urgency.

"The minister demanded that the report be submitted forthwith."
→ This is not a gentle suggestion. The minister wants it on their desk immediately, and the word forthwith makes that crystal clear.

Notice that in every example, there is someone in authority giving a serious directive. That is the natural environment of this word.
An Important Nuance You Should Know

In everyday usage, forthwith simply means this very moment. However, in legal language specifically, courts have sometimes interpreted forthwith to mean "as soon as is reasonably possible" rather than literally at this instant — because the real world sometimes requires a small amount of time even when urgency is at its maximum.

For example, if a court orders a prisoner released "forthwith," the actual release might still take a few hours because paperwork must be processed. But the word makes clear that every unnecessary delay is unacceptable. You must act with the highest possible urgency and eliminate all avoidable waiting.

This does not change the word's fundamental meaning. It simply acknowledges that "immediately" in a practical sense sometimes means "with the least humanly possible delay," not "in zero seconds."
How It Compares to Similar Words

Several words share the idea of urgency, but they sit at different levels of formality:

"Right away" is informal and conversational. You say it to a friend.

"Immediately" is neutral — appropriate in both casual and formal settings. It is the everyday workhorse of urgency.

"At once" is slightly formal and sharp. It feels more serious than "right away."

"Forthwith" is the most formal of all. It is the language of official commands, legal orders, and serious authority. It is not a word you stumble into — when it appears, it has been placed there deliberately to signal the highest level of seriousness.

All of these mean "without delay," but forthwith is the one reserved for the most weighty, official, and commanding situations.

It is worth being clear about what forthwith does not mean, because learners sometimes confuse words of urgency with words of nearness.

Forthwith does not mean:

  • Soon
  • Shortly
  • In a little while
  • When you get a chance
  • Before long

All of those allow for some delay. Forthwith allows for none. If someone uses forthwith, they are not giving you wiggle room — they are closing the door on any notion of waiting.

Forthwith = immediately, without any delay, stated in a formal and authoritative way — the language of courts, officials, and commanding authority.

When you see it, read it as: do this now, not later, with no excuses, and this is not a casual request.
